raw_case_text:
A 74-year-old male presented with history of fever and skin rash on the extremities for 1 week. Additionally, he complained of chronic diarrhea. There was no history of night sweats, cough, chest or joint pain, oral lesions, drug use, and tick bites. He lived on a farm and mowed his lawn regularly. He had recently travelled to Florida 1 month prior to admission. His past medical history was significant for previously diagnosed T-cell large granular lymphocytic leukemia, crohn's disease, rheumatoid arthritis, cytomegalovirus (CMV) colitis, and monoclonal gammopathy of uncertain significance (MGUS). He had received multiple immunosuppressive agents in the past, and was taking tofacitinib and daily prednisone at the time of presentation, in addition to valganciclovir. On admission, he was febrile (temperature 39.6 C). Bilaterally symmetrical desquamative, erythematous skin rash was seen on his hands, thighs, and lower legs in the background of generalized pitting edema. The rest of his physical examination was unremarkable.
Initial laboratory data demonstrated normocytic, normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 8.5 g/dl); normal white blood cell count (WBC 5.6 k/ul) including differentials and normal serum chemistries. His C-Reactive protein (CRP) was elevated at 29.6 mg/dl (normal = 0-1). Other relevant tests included negative blood cultures, negative fungal antibody panel in blood, negative blood CMV DNA by the polymerase chain reaction (PCR), negative Parvovirus B19 by serologies and PCR tests, and negative serum West Nile virus immunoglobulin G (IgG); and serum cryptococcal antigen, urinary histoplasma, and Legionella antigen. A subsequent computerized tomography (CT) scan of the chest demonstrated multifocal ground-glass and consolidative opacities with air bronchograms predominantly in the left upper lobe (LUL) [Figure 1a and Figure 1b]. The skin rash was biopsied; initial tissue cultures from the biopsy grew spherical unicellular yeast-like fungal organisms. On the second day of his hospital stay, the patient developed significant hypoxia and confusion, requiring endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. The patient underwent bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) from the LUL and broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy in the form of vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam was initiated. The final cultures from both the skin biopsies, taken from upper and lower extremities, as well as later blood cultures were positive for Prototheca wickerhamii, a rare opportunistic yeast-like alga. The BAL smear was also positive for yeast-like organisms morphologically similar to Prototheca wickerhamii. However, typical morula forms were not observed in BAL, so the likelihood of a fungal-mimic could not be ruled out. Prototheca wickerhamii is known to mimic yeast-like fungus on routine media. Given the patient's immunosuppressive state, lung lesions, and the sudden hypoxia with widened A-a gradient, the possibility of coinfection with. Pneumocystis jiroveci was entertained. The antimicrobial coverage was broadened to include amphotericin B and trimethoprin-sulfamethoxazole with prednisone. A PCR, performed on the BAL, confirmed the presence of Pneumocystis jirovecii. A long-term course of amphotericin B and trimethoprin-sulfamethoxazole was planned to treat the concomitant systemic protothecosis and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP). Eventually, the patient succumbed to a bacterial ventilator-associated pneumonia, and the family decided to transition him to comfort care.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 74-year-old immunosuppressed male with T-cell large granular lymphocytic leukemia, Crohn's disease, and rheumatoid arthritis presented with a 1-week history of fever and bilateral extremity skin rash alongside chronic diarrhea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, who was taking daily oral prednisone, tofacitinib, and valganciclovir following multiple prior immunosuppressive regimens, presented with 1 week of high fever and a symmetric erythematous desquamative rash over his upper and lower extremities, superimposed on chronic diarrhea. On hospital day 2, he developed acute severe hypoxemia and confusion requiring endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation.
subjective.past_medical_history: T-cell large granular lymphocytic (T-LGL) leukemia; Crohn's disease; rheumatoid arthritis; cytomegalovirus (CMV) colitis; monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS). Social and epidemiological history: Lived on a farm, mowed his lawn regularly, and had traveled to Florida 1 month prior to admission; no illicit drug use or known tick bites.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high fever, extremity skin rash, generalized edema, and chronic diarrhea (and acute hypoxia/confusion on day 2); negative for night sweats, cough, chest pain, arthralgia, or oral lesions. Home medications were tofacitinib, daily oral prednisone, and valganciclovir.

objective.physical_examination: On admission: Febrile with temperature 39.6 °C; bilaterally symmetrical desquamative, erythematous skin rash over the hands, thighs, and lower legs against a background of generalized pitting edema; remainder of initial exam unremarkable. On hospital day 2: Significant hypoxemia and confusion requiring intubation.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: Normocytic, normochromic anemia with hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL; normal WBC count (5.6 K/μL) and differential; normal serum chemistries; elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) at 29.6 mg/dL (normal: 0–1 mg/dL); widened alveolar-arterial (A-a) oxygen gradient on day 2. Negative infectious screening: Negative serum fungal antibody panel, blood CMV DNA PCR, Parvovirus B19 serology/PCR, West Nile virus IgG, serum cryptococcal antigen, and urinary Histoplasma and Legionella antigens. Skin biopsy and blood cultures: Upper and lower extremity skin biopsies and subsequent blood cultures grew spherical unicellular yeast-like organisms definitively identified as the achlorophyllous alga Prototheca wickerhamii.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT: Multifocal ground-glass and consolidative opacities with air bronchograms, predominantly in the left upper lobe (LUL). Hospital day 2 bronchoscopy with left upper lobe bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): BAL smear showed yeast-like organisms morphologically similar to Prototheca wickerhamii (without classic morula forms); BAL polymerase chain reaction (PCR) tested positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Concomitant disseminated Prototheca wickerhamii infection (cutaneous, bloodstream, and pulmonary protothecosis confirmed by upper/lower extremity skin biopsy cultures, blood cultures, and BAL smear) and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP; confirmed by positive BAL PCR, left upper lobe ground-glass/consolidative opacities on chest CT, and acute hypoxemic respiratory failure with widened A-a gradient) in a patient receiving tofacitinib and prednisone for T-LGL leukemia, Crohn's disease, and rheumatoid arthritis. Plan and clinical course: Intubated on hospital day 2 and initially started on empiric vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam, then broadened to intravenous amphotericin B (for systemic protothecosis) plus trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and prednisone (for PJP). Despite targeted therapy, he subsequently developed a secondary bacterial ventilator-associated pneumonia, was transitioned to comfort care by his family, and died.
